newsitem.title: USA: After December, players eye Penn Traffic Jan sales.
newsitem.headline: After December, players eye Penn Traffic Jan sales.

text.p: Corporate bond players are expected to keep a watchful eye on Penn Traffic's release of comparable store sales for January as rumors of bankruptcy circulated the market following December's weak report.
The company, a food retailer in the eastern U.S., said it would announce its fourth quarter earnings and same-store sales on February 12. It had no further comment.
Same-store sales for December fell 8.5 percent.

"The bonds got hit hard when December same-store sales came out and when they were at the absolute bottom rumors circulated of a bankruptcy filing," one trader of distressed credits said. "However, the company did not file and the bonds have managed to retrace some losses simply because of the relief factor."
Reports of suppliers cutting back credit and demanding cash on delivery exacerbated the selling, traders said.
Meanwhile, Penn Traffic 11.50 percent senior notes due 2001 were better bid at 87 compared with lows near 78 after last month's report.

"Penn Traffic bonds have been strengthening over the past couple of days incrementally a 1/2 point here, a 1/2 point there, reversing the bloodbath of the last couple of weeks," said one high-yield trader.

"The 9.625 percent bonds traded as low as a 30 bid following (December's sales), but are now at 34 on the board," the trader added. "They have retraced some of their losses, but keep in mind that they were at 40."

Separately, the company forecast in its January 27 news release that its earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) performance would be the highest of any quarter this fiscal year.
The company saw fourth quarter EBITDA between $49 million and $52 million.
"Not until the numbers get better will they be credible," said Sheila McNeely, an analyst with KDP Investment Advisors Inc. "The bonds are trading 30 cents on the dallar."

When asked about Penn Traffic bankruptcy rumors McNeely replied: "There's a good chance of that happening. The banks need to stay involved, they need to continue to loan money to the company and the company needs to be able to maintain its covenants, but have continued to break those."
She noted the company already has fourteen amendments to its bank covenants.
